live.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
live.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL: a threat actor tracked under many names
live.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL is the Secureworks name for an actor also known as Kimsuky and APT43. The catalogue lists its aliases and tools. No public report in this library describes its operations.

sentences.t: NICKEL KIMBALL is the name Secureworks uses for this threat actor.
Other vendors track it under many other names, including APT43, Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, THALLIUM, TA427 and Black Banshee.
The catalogue lists eight tools tied to the actor: BabyShark, FastFire, FastSpy, FireViewer, KONNI, KimJongRAT, Kimsuky and ReconShark.
No public report in this library describes its operations.

next.name: NICKEL KIMBALL
next.headline: NICKEL KIMBALL (Kimsuky): a North Korea-linked espionage group focused on South Korea
next.in_short: NICKEL KIMBALL, better known as Kimsuky, is tracked by many vendors under many names. Reports describe phishing, trojanized installers and ClickFix lures, mostly aimed at South Korean targets. Attribution varies in confidence.

sentences.t: Secureworks tracks this actor as NICKEL KIMBALL. The catalogue lists other names, including Kimsuky, APT43, Emerald Sleet, Velvet Chollima, THALLIUM and Springtail.

Symantec describes Springtail, also known as Kimsuky, as a North Korean espionage group. It says the US government has described the group as a unit of North Korea's military intelligence organization.
Naming is not settled. According to the Sekoia and Kudelski Security overview, some DPRK experts regard Kimsuky as a mega-cluster with several branches, such as TA406 and TA408.
Genians notes that some researchers class KONNI, Kimsuky and APT37 as one group. It also cites the MSMT report, which assesses Kimsuky and KONNI as distinct groups.
Microsoft says it saw Kimsuky target people in international affairs organizations, NGOs, government agencies and media companies. It describes these as limited attacks since January 2025.
South Korea's National Police Agency said Kimsuky exploited an email server flaw at a defense subcontractor between April and July 2023.
In July 2022, AhnLab's ASEC team reported signs of AppleSeed being spread to maintenance contractors of a military unit. ASEC calls AppleSeed a backdoor mainly used by Kimsuky.

A December 2022 article said officials believed hackers operating from North Korea breached the KAERI nuclear research agency through a VPN flaw. One of the thirteen IP addresses involved was linked to infrastructure used by Kimsuky.

In a January 2021 report, ESTsecurity researchers said Thallium targeted users of a private stock investment messenger service. They said it was unclear whether the aim was money or spying on traders.

Microsoft says Kimsuky adopted ClickFix-style tactics. A target gets a spear-phishing PDF from a fake South Korean official and is told to run attacker-supplied code in PowerShell as administrator. That installs a browser-based remote desktop tool.

AhnLab reports Kimsuky spreading the PebbleDash backdoor mainly through spear-phishing with shortcut files disguised as documents. The chain uses PowerShell, a Dropbox and TCP socket command channel, and a patched system DLL to bypass RDP authentication.

Symantec says Springtail has focused on Trojanized software installers. It also reports a Linux backdoor, Linux.Gomir, that appears to be a Linux version of the GoBear backdoor and supports 17 commands.

ENKI WhiteHat attributes new DOCSWAP Android apps to Kimsuky, citing shared infrastructure, a known phishing string and Korean comments. It calls this strong evidence, not definitive confirmation. The apps log keystrokes through accessibility services.
S2W suspects an earlier DocSwap sample is a possible connection to Kimsuky. S2W tracks its operators as puNK-004.

South Korea's National Cyber Security Center says Kimsuky compromised a construction trade organisation's website in January 2024. Trojanized security installers, signed with a valid certificate, were then distributed.

Genians assesses with moderate confidence that a campaign using NodeLinkRAT against South Korean policy and security professionals was Kimsuky. It began with reply-based spearphishing posing as a National Assembly member's aide. Genians says a third party imitating the techniques cannot be ruled out.
Breakglass Intelligence attributes an exposed command server to Kimsuky with high confidence. It maps about 79 domains and describes Naver and tax-themed lures aimed at South Korean users.
Be wary of any message that asks you to run commands, enable macros or install a security tool to read a document. Check such requests through a separate channel before acting.
